payload.prompt: Which workplace use is a speech recognition scenario?

options.text: Transcribing a customer call into searchable text
options.rationale: This is speech recognition because the system listens to spoken language and converts it into text. The searchable record is created from audio input.

options.text: Reading a policy document aloud to an employee
options.rationale: This describes speech synthesis, because written text is turned into spoken audio. It does not involve converting speech into text.
options.better_fit: This would be correct for speech synthesis scenarios such as accessibility tools or document readers.

options.text: Speaking a GPS navigation instruction
options.rationale: A GPS voice instruction is generated speech from stored or computed text. The system is speaking rather than listening to a user.
options.better_fit: This fits speech synthesis for navigation or alerting systems.

options.text: Confirming a driver command after hearing it
options.rationale: This includes both listening to a command and speaking a confirmation. Because both directions are involved, it is not recognition alone.
options.better_fit: This would be correct for combined speech interactions in vehicles.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech recognition turns spoken input into text or commands.

payload.prompt: Which scenarios primarily use speech synthesis? Select all that apply.

options.text: A navigation app speaks the next turn
options.rationale: The app generates spoken instructions from route information. This is speech synthesis because the output is audio.

options.text: An accessibility tool reads a document aloud
options.rationale: The tool turns written content into spoken audio. That is a standard synthesis scenario for accessibility.

options.text: A meeting platform creates a transcript from discussion
options.rationale: A transcript from spoken discussion requires converting audio into text. That is speech recognition, not synthesis.
options.better_fit: This would be correct for speech recognition scenarios in meetings.

options.text: A call center analyzes caller sentiment from audio
options.rationale: Sentiment analysis depends on understanding spoken customer input. It does not generate speech from text.
options.better_fit: This fits speech recognition in customer service analytics.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Synthesis scenarios produce spoken audio.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Reading text aloud is a synthesis scenario.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: An accessibility use of synthesis is missed.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A core productivity benefit is overlooked.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Recognition can reduce manual effort when speech must become text.

payload.prompt: Evaluate this statement.
payload.statement: An IVR system can combine spoken prompts with caller speech input.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The two-way nature of IVR is missed.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Combined speech interactions listen and speak within the same flow.

payload.prompt: Why is reading a document aloud considered speech synthesis?

options.text: The system converts written text into spoken audio
options.rationale: Speech synthesis produces speech from text. A document reader starts with written content and outputs audio.

options.text: The system converts a meeting discussion into notes
options.rationale: Meeting notes from spoken discussion are created through speech recognition. The input is audio, not written text.
options.better_fit: This would fit speech recognition scenarios for meetings and interviews.

options.text: The system detects caller sentiment during a support call
options.rationale: Sentiment analysis on a call depends on interpreting spoken customer input. It is not the generation of spoken output from text.
options.better_fit: This fits speech recognition scenarios in customer service analytics.

options.text: The system routes a caller based on spoken words
options.rationale: Routing based on what a caller says requires recognizing speech input. Speech synthesis may speak menu options, but the routing decision comes from listening.
options.better_fit: This would be correct for speech recognition in call routing.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Speech synthesis is the speaking side of the interaction.

payload.prompt: Which statements explain why IVR is a combined speech interaction? Select all that apply.

options.text: It may listen to a caller's spoken choice
options.rationale: Listening to a spoken choice is the recognition side of IVR. The caller's voice becomes input for routing or selection.

options.text: It may speak menu options or confirmations
options.rationale: Speaking options or confirmations is the synthesis side of IVR. The system generates audio for the caller.

options.text: It only creates written meeting records
options.rationale: Creating written meeting records is a meeting transcription use case. IVR is a phone interaction with spoken prompts and responses.
options.better_fit: This would fit speech recognition for workplace meetings.

options.text: It is limited to generating media voiceovers
options.rationale: Media voiceovers are a synthesis scenario, but IVR is not limited to media production. IVR is a two-way phone service pattern.
options.better_fit: This would fit speech synthesis in entertainment, podcasts, or training videos.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. IVR combines listening and speaking.

payload.prompt: A hospital wants clinicians to speak patient notes directly into an electronic health record. Which speech capability should the team choose?

options.text: Speech recognition
options.rationale: The clinicians provide spoken input that must become written patient notes. That is a direct use of speech recognition in healthcare documentation.

options.text: Speech synthesis
options.rationale: Speech synthesis would read or generate spoken audio from text. It would not capture dictated notes into the health record.
options.better_fit: Speech synthesis would fit a tool that reads discharge instructions aloud to patients.

feedback.intrinsic: The notes are not captured as structured text in the record.
feedback.instructional: When the system listens and turns speech into text, choose speech recognition.

options.text: Combined speech interaction
options.rationale: A combined interaction would both listen and speak back. The stated goal is dictation into a record, so spoken output is not required.
options.better_fit: Combined speech would fit a clinical assistant that accepts a spoken request and replies with spoken guidance.

feedback.intrinsic: The design becomes more complex than the dictation workflow needs.
feedback.instructional: Use combined speech only when both spoken input and spoken output are central to the task.

options.text: Voice-only customer service
options.rationale: Voice-only customer service is a business application, not the underlying capability needed for clinical dictation. The needed capability is converting speech to text.
options.better_fit: This would fit a support channel where callers complete service tasks by voice.

feedback.intrinsic: The hospital still lacks the dictation capability for patient notes.
feedback.instructional: Match the capability to the data flow: spoken notes becoming text require recognition.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Dictating clinical notes into records is a speech recognition scenario.

payload.prompt: An e-learning team needs each lesson script turned into narrated audio for learners. Which option is the best fit?

options.text: Speech synthesis
options.rationale: The team starts with lesson text and needs spoken narration. Speech synthesis is designed to produce audio from written content.

options.text: Speech recognition
options.rationale: Speech recognition would turn learner speech or recorded audio into text. It does not create narration from a script.
options.better_fit: Speech recognition would fit a pronunciation practice activity that listens to learners.

feedback.intrinsic: The team ends up with transcripts or commands, not narrated lessons.
feedback.instructional: When the output must be spoken audio generated from text, choose speech synthesis.

options.text: Call sentiment analysis
options.rationale: Sentiment analysis evaluates spoken or transcribed conversations. It does not generate lesson narration.
options.better_fit: This would fit a customer service team analyzing caller emotions.

feedback.intrinsic: The lesson script remains silent and unusable as narration.
feedback.instructional: Select the speech use case that directly transforms the available input into the desired output.

options.text: IVR routing
options.rationale: IVR routing guides callers through spoken menu flows. It is not a production tool for narrated learning content.
options.better_fit: This would fit a phone system that listens to callers and speaks menu choices.

feedback.intrinsic: Learners do not receive narrated lesson audio.
feedback.instructional: E-learning narration is a synthesis scenario because text becomes speech.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Narrated lessons are a common speech synthesis scenario.

payload.prompt: A car system must understand a spoken request to change temperature and then say, 'Temperature set to 20 degrees.' Which design should be selected?

options.text: A combined speech interaction
options.rationale: The system must recognize the driver's spoken command and synthesize a spoken confirmation. Both directions are essential to the user experience.

options.text: Speech recognition only
options.rationale: Recognition would understand the temperature request but would not provide the spoken confirmation. The scenario explicitly requires the system to speak back.
options.better_fit: Recognition only would fit silent command execution or transcription.

feedback.intrinsic: The driver may not know whether the temperature command was accepted.
feedback.instructional: Choose combined speech when the workflow requires both listening and speaking.

options.text: Speech synthesis only
options.rationale: Synthesis could speak the confirmation but would not understand the driver's command. The system first needs to process spoken input.
options.better_fit: Synthesis only would fit prewritten alerts or GPS directions.

feedback.intrinsic: The system can announce information but cannot act on the driver command.
feedback.instructional: A two-way voice flow needs recognition for input and synthesis for output.

options.text: Manual note-taking reduction
options.rationale: Reducing note-taking is a benefit in documentation settings, not the interaction design for a vehicle command. It does not specify the listening and speaking capabilities needed.
options.better_fit: This would fit meeting transcription or healthcare documentation benefits.

feedback.intrinsic: The vehicle workflow lacks a concrete speech design.
feedback.instructional: Business value describes why a system matters; the scenario asks which speech capability pattern to use.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Vehicle command confirmation is a two-way voice interaction.

payload.prompt: A contact center wants to improve live calls by routing callers from spoken requests and creating real-time text for agents. Which capabilities should the design include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Speech recognition for spoken request routing
options.rationale: Routing based on what callers say requires recognizing spoken input. The system must interpret speech to choose the right destination.

options.text: Real-time transcription for agent-visible text
options.rationale: Creating text during a live call is a recognition scenario. It gives agents a readable stream or record of the conversation.

options.text: Speech synthesis for narrated e-learning lessons
options.rationale: Narrated lessons are generated from scripts for learners, not from live caller speech for agents. This option does not support routing or live transcription.
options.better_fit: This would fit an e-learning team producing spoken course audio.

feedback.intrinsic: Agents still cannot see live call text or route callers from spoken requests.
feedback.instructional: For live spoken input that becomes text or decisions, use recognition-oriented capabilities.

options.text: Character voice generation for entertainment
options.rationale: Character voice generation creates synthetic voices for media. It does not interpret live customer speech or produce call transcripts.
options.better_fit: This would fit a game or animation production workflow.

feedback.intrinsic: The contact center problem remains unsolved.
feedback.instructional: Plausible speech tools must still match the workplace scenario and desired outcome.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Routing from speech and live text both depend on recognition.

payload.prompt: A public transit app must announce service alerts and read route changes aloud when riders cannot look at their phones. Which speech synthesis benefits apply? Select all that apply.

options.text: Important information reaches users without requiring screen attention
options.rationale: Spoken alerts help riders receive information when looking at a screen is inconvenient or unsafe. This is a core value of speech synthesis notifications.

options.text: Written route updates become spoken audio
options.rationale: The app starts with text-based route information and outputs speech. That conversion is speech synthesis.

options.text: Caller sentiment is analyzed from support calls
options.rationale: Caller sentiment analysis examines speech input in service conversations. It does not describe announcing transit updates aloud.
options.better_fit: This would fit customer service speech recognition analytics.

feedback.intrinsic: The app gains no way to speak urgent rider updates.
feedback.instructional: Synthesis benefits focus on spoken output from information the system already has.

options.text: Clinicians dictate patient notes into records
options.rationale: Clinical dictation converts spoken notes into written records. The transit app needs the reverse direction: route text to spoken audio.
options.better_fit: This would fit healthcare documentation using speech recognition.

feedback.intrinsic: The rider notification problem is not addressed.
feedback.instructional: Check whether the system is listening to users or speaking information to them.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Transit alerts are a synthesis use because the system speaks information.

payload.prompt: A voice assistant for office workers should accept spoken calendar commands and answer aloud with the scheduled time. Which components are required? Select all that apply.

options.text: Speech recognition to understand spoken calendar commands
options.rationale: The assistant must listen to the user's command and interpret it. That requires recognition of spoken input.

options.text: Speech synthesis to speak the scheduled time
options.rationale: The assistant must produce an audible answer. Speaking the scheduled time is synthesis.

options.text: Only transcript storage with no spoken response
options.rationale: Transcript storage might capture speech, but it does not answer aloud. The scenario requires a two-way assistant experience.
options.better_fit: This would fit compliance recording or searchable meeting records.

feedback.intrinsic: The worker gives a command but receives no spoken confirmation.
feedback.instructional: A voice assistant that listens and replies needs both recognition and synthesis.

options.text: Only prewritten audio alerts with no listening
options.rationale: Prewritten alerts can speak information but cannot understand calendar commands. The assistant must process user speech first.
options.better_fit: This would fit notification systems that announce fixed updates.

feedback.intrinsic: The assistant cannot schedule anything from the user's voice.
feedback.instructional: Spoken output alone is not enough when the user must control the system by voice.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. A spoken command plus spoken answer requires both components.

payload.prompt: A support leader compares two proposals: one transcribes calls for later search, and another speaks automated status updates to customers. Which evaluation is most accurate?

options.text: The first mainly improves records, while the second reduces the need to look at a screen
options.rationale: Call transcription creates searchable records from conversations. Spoken status updates help customers receive information without reading a screen.

options.text: Both proposals mainly create character voices for entertainment
options.rationale: Character voices are a speech synthesis use in entertainment, but neither proposal is about fictional voices. The proposals target support records and customer notifications.
options.better_fit: This would fit game, animation, or media production scenarios using speech synthesis.

feedback.intrinsic: The business case mislabels operational support tools as entertainment features.

options.text: The first proposal is speech synthesis, and the second is speech recognition
options.rationale: Transcribing calls depends on recognizing speech. Speaking automated updates depends on synthesis.
options.better_fit: The reversed mapping would be correct only if the first spoke text and the second listened to customer speech.

feedback.intrinsic: The technology choices would be assigned to the wrong teams.

options.text: Neither proposal creates business value because speech is only useful for accessibility
options.rationale: Accessibility is one important value, but speech also supports records, response accuracy, customer effort reduction, and production efficiency. Both proposals have plausible business value.
options.better_fit: Accessibility-focused evaluation would be appropriate for screen reader or dyslexia support projects.

feedback.intrinsic: Useful operational benefits are dismissed before analysis.
feedback.instructional: Business value includes inclusion, efficiency, records, reduced effort, and cost reduction.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The value differs by whether the system listens or speaks.

payload.prompt: A product team wants a language learning feature that listens to a learner's pronunciation and then gives spoken corrective feedback. Which classification is best?

options.text: Combined speech interaction
options.rationale: The feature listens to learner speech and then speaks feedback. That combination makes it a two-way speech application.

options.text: Speech recognition scenario only
options.rationale: Recognition is needed to evaluate pronunciation, but the feature also gives spoken feedback. The spoken response means synthesis is also part of the design.
options.better_fit: Recognition only would fit scoring pronunciation and showing written feedback silently.

feedback.intrinsic: The spoken coaching requirement is left out of the design.
feedback.instructional: When a scenario includes listening plus spoken response, classify it as combined speech.

options.text: Speech synthesis scenario only
options.rationale: Synthesis can produce feedback audio, but it cannot evaluate the learner's pronunciation by itself. The system must first recognize or analyze speech input.
options.better_fit: Synthesis only would fit playing pronunciation examples from text.

feedback.intrinsic: The system can speak examples but cannot respond to the learner's actual pronunciation.
feedback.instructional: Synthesis handles spoken output; learner speech input requires recognition.

options.text: Healthcare documentation
options.rationale: Healthcare documentation involves clinicians dictating patient notes into records. The language learning feature is about practice and feedback.
options.better_fit: This would fit a hospital dictation workflow using speech recognition.

feedback.intrinsic: The team chooses a domain pattern unrelated to learner practice.
feedback.instructional: Use domain examples only when they match the user's task and interaction pattern.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Listening and spoken feedback together make the feature combined.

options.text: Generated character voices for a game prototype

options.text: Spoken GPS directions for field drivers

options.better_fit: This would fit navigation or mobile worker safety scenarios.

options.text: A chatbot voice that reads support answers aloud
options.rationale: A speaking chatbot may reduce customer effort, but it does not create meeting notes. It is a synthesis solution for a different workflow.
options.better_fit: This would fit customer self-service where users benefit from spoken answers.

feedback.intrinsic: The funded project misses the internal productivity target.
feedback.instructional: Business value must be tied to the specific pain point named in the scenario.

payload.prompt: A bank is evaluating a voice-driven customer service system. It must let callers state their problem, route them correctly, and speak the next step. Which conclusions are valid? Select all that apply.

options.text: The system needs recognition to interpret the caller's stated problem
options.rationale: Routing depends on understanding the caller's spoken words. That is the recognition side of the system.

options.text: The system needs synthesis to speak the next step
options.rationale: Speaking instructions or confirmations requires generated audio. That is the synthesis side of the system.

options.text: The system is synthesis only because it speaks to callers
options.rationale: The system does speak, but it also listens to the caller's problem. Classifying it as synthesis only misses the routing input.
options.better_fit: Synthesis only would fit one-way spoken alerts or prerecorded-style updates generated from text.

feedback.intrinsic: The bank underestimates the listening capability needed for routing.
feedback.instructional: Evaluate every required direction of communication before classifying the speech pattern.

options.text: The system is recognition only because it routes callers
options.rationale: Routing uses recognition, but the system must also speak the next step. That spoken response requires synthesis.
options.better_fit: Recognition only would fit silent call transcription or internal routing support without audible replies.

feedback.intrinsic: Callers may be routed but not told what happens next.
feedback.instructional: A two-way customer service flow is combined when it listens and speaks.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Voice-driven service often combines recognition and synthesis.

payload.prompt: A media team must lower production costs for training videos while maintaining spoken narration and pronunciation examples. Which speech synthesis conclusions are valid? Select all that apply.

options.text: Speech synthesis can reduce narration production effort
options.rationale: Generated narration can reduce the time and cost of producing spoken training content. This aligns with lower e-learning and media production costs.

options.text: Speech synthesis can provide consistent pronunciation examples
options.rationale: Synthesis can generate spoken examples from text. That makes it useful in training and language instruction.

options.text: Speech recognition is the main tool because the team starts with scripts
options.rationale: Starting with scripts and needing speech points to synthesis. Recognition would be used if the team needed to turn spoken recordings into text.
options.better_fit: Recognition would fit transcribing recorded interviews for editing.

feedback.intrinsic: The team chooses a tool that creates text instead of narration.
feedback.instructional: When text is the input and audio is the output, synthesis is the better fit.

options.text: Call routing is the main benefit because videos need customer queues
options.rationale: Call routing is useful in contact centers, not training video production. It does not address narration cost or pronunciation examples.
options.better_fit: Call routing would fit a customer service system that handles spoken caller requests.

feedback.intrinsic: The production cost problem remains unsolved.
feedback.instructional: Keep business value tied to the actual workflow being evaluated.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. Synthesis can reduce production effort and create spoken examples.

payload.prompt: A compliance team reviews a meeting assistant that captions live discussion, lists action items, and creates a searchable record. Which evaluations are valid? Select all that apply.

options.text: It uses speech recognition because spoken discussion becomes text
options.rationale: Captions and searchable records come from converting speech into text. That is speech recognition.

options.text: It provides business value by reducing manual note-taking
options.rationale: Automatic action items and records reduce the need for people to type notes during meetings. This is a recognized business value of speech recognition.

options.text: It uses speech synthesis because captions are visible words
options.error_type: Confuses text output with speech output
options.rationale: Captions are text created from speech, so they are recognition output. Synthesis would generate spoken audio from text.
options.better_fit: Synthesis would fit reading meeting summaries aloud after the meeting.

feedback.intrinsic: The technology is misclassified, which can lead to the wrong implementation plan.
feedback.instructional: Visible text produced from spoken audio is recognition, not synthesis.

options.text: It mainly improves entertainment voice acting
options.rationale: The assistant supports workplace documentation and compliance. Entertainment voice acting is unrelated to captions, action items, or searchable records.
options.better_fit: This would fit synthesis for character voices in media production.

feedback.intrinsic: The compliance benefits are ignored.
feedback.instructional: Assess value in the setting named by the scenario: meetings, records, and note-taking.

payload.feedback_for_correct: Correct. The assistant is recognition-focused and valuable for documentation.

flashcards.back: Speech recognition turns calls into text records.
Speech synthesis creates spoken audio from text.
A system where callers speak and hear guided options.
It reduces manual note-taking and saves transcription time.
